paras: The lynching of Dr. G. H. Thomas was the killing by a mob of a man who called himself Dr. G. H. Thomas, near Oxford, Mississippi, in the early hours of July 17, 1888, after he had been arrested and placed under guard at the farm where he boarded. He was accused of drugging and "ruining" Amelia Shives, his host's daughter, whom he had treated as a physician. Wire reports told the story as the lynching of "a Rapist," but a meeting of citizens east of Oxford condemned the killing as done "without cause or provocation" and called for an investigation.

About a month before his death, the man took board with the family of Allen Shives, a farmer about ten miles east of Oxford. He presented himself as a physician, a Christian and a "world's historian," and according to a Memphis special to the Louisville Courier-Journal he won the family's full confidence. The same correspondent wrote that he offered to treat Miss Shives, who was ill, without charge. The reports charged that on Saturday, July 14, he used "wiles and drugs" to accomplish her ruin, and the Courier-Journal said she had been "mesmerized, drugged and outraged."

Thomas was arrested and, by the account of one of his guards, M. Hawkins, demanded a trial, which was set for the next day before Esquire Smith, the magistrate of the beat. Because some witnesses were too feeble to travel to Oxford, Sheriff Matthews kept him chained to a wagon at the Shives place, guarded only by Hawkins and the sheriff's nephew James Matthews.

At about two o'clock, Hawkins wrote, six or seven men surrounded the guards, searched him at pistol point and ordered him to leave, then tied Thomas with a plow line and hurried him away. Shots followed, and the body was found the next day. The wire reports put the hour at 1 o'clock and the mob at forty or "about fifty men from the east," and said Thomas was hanged to a tree and his body "riddled with bullets." The Courier-Journal added that he had to be dragged the last hundred yards.

Hawkins said that he and the other guard reported the seizure at once to a neighbor, Dave Butler, and that he helped find and bury the body. The Courier-Journal reported that the sheriff later found wigs and a false beard in the lining of Thomas's coat.

On July 30 a meeting at Philadelphia Church, fifteen miles east of Oxford, resolved that the "wilful and malicious lynching" near Pine Hill church should be investigated at once and pledged to help bring the guilty to punishment. In August Hawkins answered "parties disposed to censure the guards" with a public letter saying he recognized none of the mob, that there had been no threats, and that the sheriff had not expected violence. No report of an inquest, an arrest or a trial appears in the coverage.

The first reports came through Memphis: an Oxford special to the Memphis Avalanche dated July 17 ran in the Grenada Gazette on July 26, and a Memphis dispatch of July 19 appeared the same day in the Emporia Weekly News of Kansas under the headline "A Ravisher Lynched." The Weekly Courier-Journal ran a longer Memphis special under "Dragged to the Gallows" and "Particulars of the Lynching of a Rapist," calling Thomas "the imposter" and dwelling on sympathy for Miss Shives, who was "held blameless." The Brookhaven Leader gave the case a single line in its state news column, and none of the reports named Thomas's race.

The local Oxford Eagle printed a different view: resolutions signed by 104 citizens called the killing "one of the most outrageous and brutal" known in the country and demanded of the Courier-Journal "his authority" for its article.

The charge against Thomas rests on the Memphis and Oxford dispatches; the citizens' resolutions called the lynching "without cause or provocation" but did not say what they knew of the accusation. The mob's size also differs: forty men, about fifty, or six or seven according to Hawkins, the only eyewitness in the coverage, who wrote to defend the guards.

reader.title: Lynching of Dr. G. H. Thomas
bases: A mob took Thomas from his guards while he awaited a magistrate's trial and hanged and shot him (A2, A4, A6).

Thomas was seized from two guards by a group of at least six or seven men (forty or fifty in the wires) and hanged and shot (A2, A4, A6); the wires tied the killing to the charge that he had ruined Miss Shives (A1, A4), and local citizens called it a 'lynching' and lawlessness (A5).

An Oxford special (A4), a separate Memphis special (A1) and the local guard's letter (A6) agree that Thomas was taken from guards and killed; the citizens' resolutions (A5) dispute the provocation, not the killing.

accounts.label: Memphis and Oxford wire reports
accounts.gist: Thomas, an impostor, drugged and ruined Miss Shives; a mob of forty or fifty took him from his guard about 1 o'clock and hanged him, riddling his body with bullets.

accounts.label: Guard's letter (M. Hawkins)
accounts.gist: Six or seven men surrounded the two guards about 2 a.m., disarmed and dismissed Hawkins, tied Thomas with a plow line and took him off; shots followed and the body was found next day. Hawkins says no one expected a mob.

accounts.label: Philadelphia Church citizens' resolutions
accounts.gist: The lynching was 'wilful and malicious' and 'without cause or provocation'; the authorities should investigate and the Courier-Journal should give its authority for its article.

framing.detail: Headline 'Dragged to the Gallows. Particulars of the Lynching of a Rapist', calls Thomas 'the imposter' and stresses indignation at 'the wrong done her'.
Headline 'A Ravisher Lynched'; describes 'his wicked wiles and drugs' and the body 'left swinging'.
One line in a state news column, 'hung for villainous treatment of a young lady'.
Oxford special states the accusation as fact and reports the hanging without comment on the mob.
Local paper prints citizens' resolutions calling it 'one of the most outrageous and brutal' lynchings, with an editor's note that the signers bear responsibility.
Guard's letter calls it 'the unfortunate affair', says he would have prevented the killing, and defends the sheriff and guards against censure.
